The schedules worked differently in practice.
  • The spaced group studied more frequently
  • The massed group logged more total study time
![](images/fig2_stuydtime.png){width=80%} Because total study time was not perfectly balanced, the results should be interpreted as **descriptive patterns**, not a strict test of spacing alone. ## XP Results XP told two different stories.
  • Massed shows higher XP per session
  • Spaced shows higher XP per minute
![](images/fig3_xp.png){width=80%} XP reflects app activity, not language proficiency. ## Weekly Engagement Study behavior changed over time. ![](images/fig4_weeklyengagement.png){width=80%} A good study routine needs to be sustainable, not just effective on a single day. ## Test Results Participants completed a Swedish proficiency test with four sections: - Grammar I - Grammar II - Vocabulary - Reading ### Overall - Highest performance: **Reading (57.2%)** - Overall mean: **49.3%** ### By Group
  • The spaced group outperformed the massed group across all dimensions
  • The advantage was especially strong in vocabulary
![](images/fig5_testperformance.png){width=80%} ## Summary - Spaced learning showed a consistent advantage - The largest effect appeared in vocabulary - Results are descriptive, with individual differences
![](images/fig8_Duo.png){width=40px} Key Take Away:
  • Study frequency matters
  • Longer sessions produce more XP per session
  • XP is not the same as learning
  • Multiple metrics give a better picture
  • Short repeated practice may support vocabulary learning
